title: Probability: Outcomes and Simple Experiments
seo_title: Grade 5 Probability Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Perform simple repeated events and list possible outcomes for experiments such as tossing a coin, rolling a die and spinning a spinner; list possible outcomes for experiments; count and compare the frequency of actual outcomes for a series of up to 20 trials.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 5 probability worksheets: outcomes, likely and unlikely events, comparing chances and experiments. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Count the ways each outcome can happen.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • An outcome is a possible result. A coin has 2 outcomes; a dice has 6.
  • Use words like impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.
  • In an experiment, record the results with tallies. Do at least 20 trials.
  • The results of an experiment are close to the prediction, but not always the same.

Examples

Example

A spinner: 6 red parts and 2 blue parts

6 parts out of 8 are red

Answer: red is more likely

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
All equally likelyCount how many ways each can happen.
It is dueA coin has no memory.
Exact matchResults vary.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 5 say about probability?
faq.a: Perform simple repeated events and list possible outcomes, and count and compare the actual outcomes for experiments with up to 20 trials.
One go of the experiment, like one flip of a coin.

faq.q: Is getting 6 on a dice likely?
faq.a: No, it is unlikely: 1 out of 6.
More trials give a better picture.

items.q: You toss a coin. Which list shows all the possible outcomes?
items.e: A coin can land on heads or tails. List each outcome once. “1 out of 2” is the chance of one outcome, not a list of outcomes.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The dice can land on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. That is 6 outcomes. There is no 0 on a dice, so not 7. Only one number comes up each roll, but there are 6 possible ones.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which number is NOT a possible outcome?
items.e: A dice shows 1 to 6. 7 can never come up.

items.q: Which list shows all the possible outcomes of this spinner?
items.e: The spinner can land on any of its 4 numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4. 5 is not on the spinner.

items.q: Which experiment has exactly 2 possible outcomes?
c: picking a day of the week
items.e: A coin has 2 outcomes: heads or tails. A dice has 6, the days of the week 7 and the spinner 4. So the answer is tossing a coin.

items.q: Which list shows all the possible outcomes of this spinner?
items.e: Red appears twice, but it is still only one outcome. List it once: red, blue, green.

items.q: A bag has 4 green and 4 white marbles. You take one without looking. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: The outcome is a colour, so there are 2 outcomes: green or white. 8 is the number of marbles.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one card. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: Any card from 1 to 10 can be picked: that is 10 outcomes. There is no card 0, so not 11.

items.q: Which experiment has 7 possible outcomes?
c: picking a month of the year
picking a day of the week
items.e: There are 7 days in a week, so picking a day of the week has 7 outcomes. A dice has 6, the months 12 and a coin 2.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which list shows all the even outcomes?
items.e: The even numbers on a dice are 2, 4, 6. 1, 3, 5 are odd, and 8 is not on a dice.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The cube can land on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: 6 outcomes. 21 adds the numbers (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) instead of counting them.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which is NOT a possible outcome?
items.e: The faces show 1 to 6, so 7 can never come up. 1 and 6 are the smallest and largest faces.

items.q: You take one marble from this bag without looking. What are the possible outcomes?
items.e: Every marble is red or blue, so the outcomes are red or blue. 3 and 2 are how many of each colour, not outcomes. There is no yellow marble.

items.q: R is red, B is blue and Y is yellow. How many different colours can this spinner land on?
items.e: The spinner has 6 sections, but only 3 colours: red, blue and yellow. 6 counts the sections, not the colours.

items.q: Cards numbered 5 to 12 are shuffled. You pick one. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The cards are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12: 8 cards. 12 − 5 = 7 forgets one card. 17 adds 5 + 12.

items.q: Which outcome is impossible on this spinner?
items.e: All the numbers (2, 4, 6, 8) are even, so an odd number can never come up. 6 and 8 are greater than 5, so that can happen.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which outcomes make the event “roll a number greater than 4”?
items.e: Greater than 4 means bigger than 4, so 4 itself does not count: 5 and 6. 1, 2, 3 and 4 are the outcomes that are NOT greater than 4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which outcomes make the event “roll an even number”?
items.e: The even numbers on the cube are 2, 4 and 6. Don’t forget 6. There is no 0 on the cube. 1, 3 and 5 are odd.

items.q: Are the 4 outcomes on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, green is the most likely
Yes, all 4 sections are the same size
Yes, because every spinner is fair
No, red is at the top
items.e: Each colour has one section and all the sections are the same size, so yes: each colour is 14. Where a colour sits does not matter.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which outcome is more likely?
items.e: There are 5 green marbles and only 1 purple marble, so green is more likely. Two colours does not mean the two outcomes are equally likely.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which word describes rolling a 7?
items.e: No face shows 7, so it can never happen: impossible. Unlikely means it can happen, but probably won’t.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. Which word describes rolling a number from 1 to 6?
items.e: Every face shows a number from 1 to 6, so it happens every time: certain.

items.q: You toss a coin. Which word describes getting heads?
items.e: Heads and tails each have the same chance, so heads is equally likely to happen or not happen.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which word describes taking a blue marble?
items.e: 9 of the 10 marbles are blue, so blue is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 red marble.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. Which word describes taking a red marble?
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 marbles is red. It can happen, but probably won’t: unlikely. Impossible would mean there is no red marble at all.

items.q: Which word describes landing on red?
items.e: Red covers 34 of the spinner, more than half: likely. It is not certain, because blue can still come up.

items.q: Which word describes landing on blue?
items.e: Blue covers exactly half of the spinner, so blue is equally likely to come up or not.

items.q: Which word means the same as a probability of 0?
items.e: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen: impossible. A probability of 1 means certain.

items.q: Which event is certain?
c: Rolling a 6 on a number cube
Getting a red marble from a bag of red and blue
items.e: The days of the week always come in the same order, so Monday after Sunday is certain. The others can happen, but not every time.

items.q: Which event is impossible?
c: Taking a red marble from a bag of red and blue marbles
Landing on blue on a red and blue spinner
Rolling a 1 on a number cube
Taking a green marble from a bag of red and blue marbles
items.e: There are no green marbles in the bag, so taking green can never happen. The others can happen.

items.q: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. One captain calls “heads”. Which words best describe the chance the call is right?
items.e: Heads and tails are equally likely, 1 out of 2. That is an even chance.

items.q: The school fete raffle sells 100 tickets. Refilwe buys 1 ticket. One ticket wins. What is her chance of winning?
items.e: 1 of the 100 tickets is hers, so her chance is 1 out of 100. “Win or lose” is not 1 out of 2, because losing is much more likely.

items.q: The same raffle has 100 tickets. Lerato buys 5 tickets. What is her chance of winning?
items.e: 5 of the 100 tickets are hers, so her chance is 5 out of 100. More tickets give a better chance.

items.q: A Grade 5 class has 25 learners. The teacher picks one name from a hat. What is the chance that Ethan is picked?
items.e: Ethan’s name is 1 of the 25 names, so the chance is 1 out of 25. 24 out of 25 is the chance he is NOT picked.

items.q: A lucky dip at the school fete has 20 prizes. 4 of them are toy lions. Palesa takes one without looking. What is her chance of a toy lion?
items.e: 4 of the 20 prizes are lions: 4 out of 20. Compare with all 20 prizes, not with the 16 others. 16 out of 20 is the chance of NOT a lion.

items.q: In a board game, Dumisani needs to roll a 5 or a 6 to win. What is his chance?
items.e: 2 numbers (5 and 6) out of the 6 numbers on a dice: 2 out of 6.

items.q: Zinhle needs to roll more than 1 on a dice to move her counter. Which word best describes her chance?
items.e: More than 1 means 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: 5 out of 6. That is likely, but not certain, because she could roll a 1.

items.q: A spinner game at the school fair has 8 equal sections. One says WIN. What is the chance of winning on one spin?
items.e: 1 of the 8 equal sections is WIN, so the chance is 1 out of 8.

items.q: Lwazi picks a day of the week at random. What is the chance it is Saturday or Sunday?
items.e: There are 7 days and 2 of them are on the weekend: 2 out of 7. 2 out of 5 compares the weekend with the 5 school days, not with all 7.

items.q: A class has 13 girls and 12 boys. One name is picked from a hat. Is a girl more likely than a boy?
c: No, a boy is more likely
items.e: 13 girls and 12 boys: a girl is a little more likely. Yes, but only a little. It is not certain.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Which colour are you most likely to get?
items.e: There are 6 red, 3 blue and 1 yellow. Red has the most marbles, so red is most likely.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 7 blue and 5 green marbles. You take one without looking. Which colour are you least likely to get?
items.e: Red has the fewest marbles (2), so red is least likely. Blue is the most likely.

items.q: Every section of a spinner is red. What is the chance it lands on red?
items.e: Red is the only colour, so the spinner must land on red. It is certain.

items.q: A bag has only red and blue marbles. What is the chance of taking a yellow marble?
items.e: There are no yellow marbles in the bag, so yellow is impossible.

items.q: A bag has 9 green marbles and 1 white marble. You take one without looking. What is the chance of green?
items.e: 9 of the 10 marbles are green, so green is likely. It is not certain, because you could take the white one.

items.q: What is the chance this spinner lands on blue?
items.e: Blue covers only one quarter. It can happen, but not often: unlikely. It is not impossible, because blue is on the spinner.

items.q: Which colour is this spinner most likely to land on?
items.e: Blue covers half the spinner, the biggest part. So blue is most likely. Red starts at the top, but that does not matter.

items.q: Which number is this spinner most likely to land on?
items.e: The 6 sections are equal. 1 has 1 section, 2 has 2 sections and 3 has 3 sections. So 3 is most likely.

items.q: Which statement about this spinner is true?
c: Blue is more likely than red
Red is more likely than blue
Red and blue are equally likely
items.e: Blue covers two thirds and red one third. So blue is more likely than red. Red is less likely, but not impossible.

items.q: Which colour is this spinner least likely to land on?
items.e: Count the equal sections: blue 3, yellow 3, red 2. Red has the least, so it is least likely.

items.q: Are the 4 colours on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, green is the least likely
No, red is at the top, so it is more likely
Yes, the 4 sections are the same size
items.e: Each colour has one quarter of the spinner. Equal sections give equally likely outcomes. Where a section is does not matter.

items.q: You toss a fair coin. Are heads and tails equally likely?
c: Only if you toss it twice
items.e: A fair coin has 2 outcomes with the same chance: heads 1 out of 2, tails 1 out of 2.

items.q: You roll a fair six-sided dice. Which statement is true?
c: Even numbers are more likely than odd
items.e: Each face has the same chance, 1 out of 6. So every number is equally likely. 6 feels hard to get only because people want it.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: There are 3 red and 3 blue marbles. The same number gives the same chance, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Are the outcomes on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, red has the biggest section
No, yellow has the biggest section
Yes, there are 3 colours, so each is the same
items.e: Red covers half the spinner. Blue and yellow cover a quarter each. So red is more likely. Having 3 colours does not make them equally likely.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Are red and blue equally likely?
c: No, there are more red marbles
items.e: 5 red and 2 blue: red has more marbles, so red is more likely. Not equally likely. Two colours does not mean a 1 out of 2 chance each.

items.q: Are red and blue equally likely on this spinner?
c: Yes, each has 3 of the 6 sections
No, red is at the top
items.e: The 6 sections are the same size. Red has 3 and blue has 3, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Are red and blue equally likely on this spinner?
c: Yes, the sections are the same size
No, red has 4 of the 6 sections
items.e: The sections are equal, but red has 4 of them and blue only 2. So red is more likely: not equally likely.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Is an even number equally likely as an odd number?
c: Yes, there are 3 even and 3 odd numbers
No, there are more even numbers
items.e: Even: 2, 4, 6. Odd: 1, 3, 5. Both have 3 outcomes, so they are equally likely.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Which two colours are equally likely?
items.e: There are 4 green and 4 yellow marbles, so green and yellow are equally likely. Red has only 2.

items.q: Pieter tosses a coin 20 times. He gets 11 heads and 9 tails. What does this show?
c: Heads is more likely next time
Heads and tails came up about the same
items.e: With a fair coin you expect about 10 of each, but rarely exactly 10. 11 and 9 are close, so heads and tails came up about the same.

items.q: A fair coin lands on heads 5 times in a row. What is the chance of tails on the next toss?
items.e: The coin does not remember earlier tosses. Every toss is still 1 out of 2 for tails. Tails is not “due”.

items.q: Sibusiso has not rolled a 6 in his last 10 rolls of a fair dice. On his next roll, a 6 is…
items.e: Each roll is new. A 6 is 1 out of 6 every time, so it is just as likely as before.

items.q: Ayanda spins a red and blue spinner 40 times. Red comes up 21 times and blue the rest. How many times does blue come up?
items.e: 40 − 21 = 19. 61 comes from adding instead of subtracting.

items.q: Which colour probably has the biggest section on the spinner?
items.e: Red came up most often (14 of 25 spins), so red probably has the biggest section.

items.q: Which colour probably has the smallest section on the spinner?
items.e: Red came up least often (6 of 30 spins), so red probably has the smallest section.

items.q: What do these results suggest about the spinner?
c: Blue is the most likely colour
items.e: Blue came up 31 of 50 times, much more than red or yellow. So blue is probably the most likely colour. Yellow came up 10 times, so it is not impossible.

items.q: Which statement about these results is best?
c: 4 will come up more next time
5 is the most likely number on a dice
Each number came up about 10 times
items.e: 60 rolls ÷ 6 numbers = about 10 each. The results are all close to 10, so each number came up about 10 times. Small differences are normal.

items.q: You toss a fair coin 100 times. How many heads would you expect?
items.e: Heads is 1 out of 2, and half of 100 is 50. Results change each time, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: You roll a fair dice 60 times. About how many times would you expect to roll a 3?
items.e: A 3 is 1 out of 6. 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10. About 30 would be half the rolls.

items.q: What is theoretical probability?
c: Always 12 for every event
What happened when you did an experiment
What should happen, found by counting outcomes
Always exactly the same as the experiment
items.e: Theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting the outcomes. Experimental probability is what really happened in the trials.

items.q: Andile tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 920. 12 is the theoretical probability. 911 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Andile tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What is the theoretical probability of heads?
items.e: A coin has 2 equally likely sides, so the theoretical probability of heads is 12. 920 is the experimental probability.

items.q: Priya’s class recorded 20 spins. What is the experimental probability of red?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220. 128 compares red with blue and is greater than 1. 820 is blue.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040. 1030 compares yellow with the other 30 spins.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of red?
items.e: Red came up 9 times in 30 spins: 930. 921 compares red with the other 21 spins. 13 would be the theory for 3 equal colours.

items.q: Megan rolls a number cube 30 times and gets a 6 on 7 rolls. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 6?
items.e: A 6 came up 7 times in 30 rolls: 730. 16 is the theoretical probability. 630 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Thabo spins a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, yellow) 30 times. Red comes up 11 times. Which is true?
c: Experimental: 1130, theoretical: 13
Experimental: 1119, theoretical: 13
Experimental: 13, theoretical: 1130
items.e: The experiment gave red 11 times in 30 spins: 1130. The theory says 1 of 3 equal sections: 13. So experimental 1130, theoretical 13. They are close, because 13 = 1030.

items.q: Which result gives an experimental probability of heads that is exactly the same as the theoretical probability?
items.e: The theory says 12. 10 heads in 20 tosses gives 1020 = 12. 10 heads in 10 tosses would be 1010 = 1.

items.q: Dumisani tosses a coin 20 times. Which result is impossible?
items.e: He only tosses 20 times, so he can’t get 21 heads. 0 heads or 20 heads are very unlikely, but they can happen.

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times should he expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has a probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10. About 6 uses the number on the face.

items.q: Elna tosses a coin 100 times. How many heads should she predict?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so predict about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: Chloe spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should she expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue. About 20 thinks 2 colours means 12.

items.q: Ethan spins this spinner 80 times. About how many times should he expect green?
items.e: Green is 14 of the spinner. 80 ÷ 4 = about 20. About 40 thinks “green or not green” is 12. About 60 is for the other 3 colours.

items.q: A bag has 1 red and 4 blue marbles. Ravi takes a marble, records the colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times. About how many times should he get red?
items.e: P(red) = 15. 50 ÷ 5 = 10, so about 10. About 12 uses 14 (red compared with blue). About 40 is for blue.

items.q: Dumisani tosses a coin 20 times and gets 9 heads. What fraction of his tosses were heads?
items.e: Heads came up 9 times in 20 tosses: 920. 12 is the prediction, not the result. 911 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Naledi’s class recorded 20 spins. In what fraction of the spins did red come up?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220. 128 compares red with blue and is greater than 1. 820 is blue.

items.q: In what fraction of Sarah’s spins did red come up?
items.e: Red came up 9 times in 30 spins: 930. 921 compares red with the other 21 spins. 13 would be the prediction for 3 equal colours.

items.q: Thabo spins a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, yellow) 30 times. He predicts about 10 reds and gets 11. What does this show?
c: He will get exactly 10 next time
The result is close to the prediction
items.e: 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so about 10 reds is a good prediction. 11 is only 1 more: close to the prediction. Results are rarely exactly the same as the prediction.

items.q: Lungile spins a spinner that is half red 10 times. Red comes up only 3 times. What does this show?
c: Red should come up exactly 5 times
The chance of red must be 310
Not much: a few spins can be far from the prediction
items.e: She predicts about 5 reds in 10 spins, but with only 10 spins luck changes the results a lot. A few spins can be far from the prediction. She should do many more spins.

items.q: In a game, Karabo wins if a coin lands on heads and Thabo wins if it lands on tails. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, each has a probability of 12
No, Thabo is more likely to win
No, Karabo is more likely to win
items.e: A game is fair when every player has the same chance of winning. Heads and tails are each 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: Naledi and Sibusiso roll a number cube. Naledi wins on 1 or 2. Sibusiso wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, both of them have numbers
No, Naledi is more likely to win
No, Sibusiso is more likely to win
items.e: Naledi: 26. Sibusiso: 46. The chances are not equal, so the game is not fair: Sibusiso is more likely to win.

items.q: Dumisani wins if a number cube shows an even number. Which rule for Ethan makes the game fair?
c: Ethan wins on a 5 or a 6
Ethan wins on an odd number
Ethan wins on a number less than 6
items.e: Dumisani has 2, 4, 6: 36. Odd numbers (1, 3, 5) are also 36, so the game is fair. A 1 is only 16, and 5 or 6 is 26.

items.q: Palesa and Thabo pick a card from cards numbered 1 to 10. Palesa wins on 1 to 5. Thabo wins on 6 to 10. Is the game fair?
c: No, Thabo has the bigger numbers
Yes, each has 5 of the 10 cards
items.e: Palesa has 5 cards (1 to 5) and Thabo has 5 cards (6 to 10): 510 each. The game is fair. How big the numbers are does not matter.

items.q: Chloe wins if the spinner lands on red. Daniel wins if it lands on blue or green. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, each has a probability of 12
No, Chloe has the biggest section
items.e: Chloe: 12. Daniel: 14 + 14 = 12. Both have 12, so the game is fair.

items.q: Ayanda wins on red. Dumisani wins on blue. On yellow, nobody wins and they spin again. Is the game fair?
c: No, Ayanda is more likely to win
Yes, red and blue are each 13
No, yellow is a third player
items.e: Ayanda and Dumisani each have one equal section: 13 each. Yellow does not help either player, so the game is fair.

items.q: Palesa wins on red. Thabo wins on blue. Is the game fair?
c: No, Palesa is more likely to win
No, Thabo is more likely to win: blue has 3 sections
items.e: Red covers 12 = 48. Blue has 3 small sections: 38. 48 > 38, so Palesa is more likely to win. Look at the size of the parts, not the number of sections.

items.q: Pieter and Nadia roll a number cube. Pieter wins on a number less than 4. Nadia wins on a number greater than 4. Is the game fair?
c: No, Pieter is more likely to win
No, Nadia is more likely to win
Yes, they both have 4 in the rule
items.e: Less than 4: 1, 2, 3 (36). Greater than 4: 5, 6 (26). Pieter is more likely to win. 4 is not the middle of 1 to 6.

items.q: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue marbles. Nadia wins on red and Ravi wins on blue. How many blue marbles must be added to make the game fair?
items.e: For a fair game there must be as many blue as red: 4 blue. 4 − 2 = 2 more blue marbles. 4 is how many blue there should be in total, not how many to add.

items.q: Daniel and Ethan play with 10 cards. Daniel wins on a red card and Ethan wins on a black card. 6 cards are red and 4 are black. How many red cards must be changed to black to make the game fair?
items.e: A fair game needs 5 red and 5 black. Change 1 red card: then there are 5 red and 5 black. 2 is the difference 6 − 4, but changing one card takes one from red AND adds one to black.
